summary: Qoheleth’s opening poem: generations, sun, wind and rivers move without end, yet nothing is gained and nothing is new.

context.title: The prologue of Qoheleth
paragraphs: The speaker calls himself Qoheleth, a Hebrew title that the Greek Bible rendered Ecclesiastes, member of an assembly. [c1] The book presents him as son of David and king in Jerusalem, and ancient Jewish tradition identified him with Solomon. [c2] Many modern scholars, the Jewish Encyclopedia among them, judge from its late vocabulary that the book was written after the Exile. [c3]

These verses form the book’s prologue. [c4] They open with the cry hevel havalim, a Hebrew superlative built like holy of holies, and the same cry returns in 12:8 near the book’s close. [c5] Generations pass while the earth stands; then the sun, the wind and the rivers each go round again and again without real progress. [c6]

The poem then turns from nature to human affairs: what has been will be, and there is nothing new under the sun. [c7] Some commentators compare Stoic ideas of a recurring cycle, while others hold that Qoheleth speaks simply from experience. [c8] What looks new is only what has been forgotten, and later generations will forget us in turn. [c9]

translationNotes.summary: Hevel means breath or vapour; “vanity” comes to English through the Latin, from the Greek, and loses the picture.
translationNotes.body: Hevel first means a breath or vapour, and so whatever is fleeting and without substance. [c10] It is the same word as the name Abel, whose life was cut short. [c11] The rendering vanity comes through the Vulgate from the Septuagint, while other Greek translators wrote vapour of vapours. [c12] The word occurs more often in this short book than in all the rest of the Old Testament together. [c13]

translationNotes.summary: Qoheleth comes from the verb for calling an assembly together; “Preacher” and “Teacher” fit it only loosely.
translationNotes.body: Qoheleth is a feminine participle describing someone who calls an assembly together, used here as a name or title for a man. [c14] Older commentators proposed convener or debater instead of preacher, and the Brown-Driver-Briggs lexicon adds collector of sayings. [c15] Barnes links the title to personified Wisdom, who calls the people together in Proverbs. [c16]

translationNotes.summary: Yitron, found only in Ecclesiastes, means what remains over: the surplus on life’s balance sheet.
translationNotes.body: Yitron is found in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes. [c17] Its strict sense is what remains over, so the question asks whether any surplus is left on the balance sheet of life. [c18] The Cambridge Bible suggests it was a commercial word that came into common use after the Exile. [c19] Put as a question, the line amounts to a strong denial. [c20]

translationNotes.summary: In the Bible “under the sun” belongs to this book alone; other books say “under heaven”.
translationNotes.body: The phrase under the sun occurs some twenty-nine times in Ecclesiastes and nowhere else in the Old Testament, which says under heaven instead. [c21] It names the earth as the world of human life. [c22] The Cambridge Bible thought it Greek in character, but the Jewish Encyclopedia points to the same phrase, meaning on earth, in the Phoenician inscriptions of Eshmunazar and Tabnit, from before 300 BC. [c23]

claims.text: The author calls himself Qoheleth (Eccl 1:2), and the Septuagint rendered this Hebrew name as Ecclesiastes, literally “member of an assembly”.
Eccl 1:1 presents Qoheleth as son of David, king in Jerusalem, and the ancients (Peshitta, Targum, Talmud) identified him with Solomon.
On the evidence of its late vocabulary, including Persian loanwords, the Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) holds that the book is post-exilic and that few still hold Solomonic authorship.
Eccl 1:2-11 is the prologue of the book.
“Vanity of vanities” (hevel havalim) is a Hebrew superlative like “holy of holies”, and the cry recurs at Eccl 12:8.
Eccl 1:4-7 takes in turn the earth, the sun, the wind and the waters: generations pass while the earth stands, and the sun, wind and waters move continually with no real progress.
Eccl 1:9 applies to human events what the preceding verses said of nature: there is nothing new under the sun.
The Cambridge Bible compares Eccl 1:9 with the Stoic doctrine of a recurring cycle of events, while the Pulpit Commentary holds that Koheleth speaks merely from experience.
Eccl 1:11 explains that things seem new only because what came before has been forgotten, and the present generation will be forgotten in turn.
Hebrew hevel primarily means breath or vapour, and figuratively whatever is fleeting and perishable.
Hevel is the same word as the proper name Abel, whose life was cut short.
The English “vanity” follows the Vulgate, which followed the Septuagint, while other Greek translators rendered the phrase “vapour of vapours”.
Hevel occurs about thirty-seven times in Ecclesiastes, against about thirty-three times in all the rest of the Old Testament.
Qoheleth is a feminine participle describing a person who calls an assembly together, used in Ecclesiastes as a man’s name or title.
Commentators have proposed “Convener” or “Debater” for Qoheleth, and Brown-Driver-Briggs gives “collector (of sentences)” beside “preacher”.
Barnes connects the name Qoheleth with personified Wisdom calling the people together in Proverbs.
Yitron (“profit, advantage”) occurs in the Old Testament only in Ecclesiastes.
The strict meaning of yitron is “that which remains”, the surplus, if any, on the balance sheet of life.
The Cambridge Bible suggests that yitron was probably a word brought into common use by Jewish commerce after the Captivity.
The question form of Eccl 1:3 conveys a strong negative.
“Under the sun” occurs 29 times in Ecclesiastes and is peculiar to this book, other books saying “under heaven”.
“Under the sun” designates the earth as the world of men.
The Cambridge Bible calls the phrase Greek in character, but the Jewish Encyclopedia notes it in the Phoenician Eshmunazar and Tabnith inscriptions, not later than 300 BC, meaning “on earth”.
